stories.headline: Ebola Outbreak in DR Congo Kills 140-Plus as Health Workers Battle Misinformation
stories.summary:
An Ebola outbreak in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of Congo, has killed more than 140 confirmed victims since being declared just over a month ago. The rare Bundibugyo strain has killed roughly one in five confirmed cases, and authorities warn the virus may have been spreading undetected for months before the outbreak was formally identified. The BBC traveled to the epicenter in Mongbwalu, where health workers are treating patients at a dedicated clinic.

Authorities face significant obstacles beyond the virus itself, including deeply rooted local myths — among them a belief that the disease stems from a 'coffin curse' and that treatment centers cause harm rather than cure. Violence linked to misinformation has targeted medical facilities; a treatment tent at Mongbwalu hospital was attacked on May 21. Health officials say trust is slowly building as survivors return to their communities.

The discharge of patient Daniel Kitambala, confirmed virus-free after two negative tests, was met with singing and celebration by healthcare workers — a deliberate public signal that survival is possible. Medical director Dr. Richard Lukodu said the number of patients voluntarily seeking care has increased since the first survivor went home. The outbreak's ultimate scale remains uncertain given the likelihood of undercounted cases in a remote, conflict-affected region.

stories.headline: UK Announces Social Media Ban for Children Under 16
stories.summary:
Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced Monday that the United Kingdom will introduce legislation banning children under the age of 16 from social media platforms including TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, and X. Under the proposed law, social media companies would be legally required to verify users' ages or face substantial fines. The announcement makes Britain part of a growing international movement, following similar measures enacted in Australia.

The ban would apply broadly across major platforms and is framed by the government as a child safety measure. Starmer's announcement did not include a specific timeline for implementation beyond indicating the ban would go into effect in spring 2027. The move has drawn mixed reactions, with supporters citing protection of minors from harmful content and critics — including some British teenagers who expressed frustration publicly — questioning its enforceability and scope.

The policy represents one of the most sweeping government interventions into children's digital lives attempted by a major democracy. Technology companies and civil liberties advocates are expected to scrutinize the age-verification mechanisms required under the proposal. Details of enforcement mechanisms and appeals processes were not immediately released.

stories.headline: MLB Warns Giants Pitchers Who Wrote Bible Verses on Pride Night Hats
stories.summary:
Major League Baseball officially warned several San Francisco Giants pitchers after they wrote Bible verse references on their caps during the team's Pride Night game last week. Starting pitcher Landen Roupp was among those who inscribed scripture designations on hats that featured a rainbow-colored Giants logo, telling reporters afterward that the verse represented God's covenant and his personal faith, adding 'there's no hate at all.'

MLB chief communications officer Pat Courtney confirmed the league's action in a statement: 'The writing on the cap violates our rules, and consistent with normal practice, we have warned the players about future violations.' Critics of the warning noted that players have routinely written on caps in other circumstances without league discipline — including during the 2025 World Series, when players from both teams wrote '#51' in tribute to a Dodgers reliever whose newborn daughter died during the series.

The incident has drawn significant media attention and reignited debate about the boundaries of religious expression in professional sports and corporate-sponsored events. Supporters of the players argue the league applied an inconsistent standard by acting only when the expression related to religious faith during a Pride-themed event. The league has not publicly addressed questions about prior instances of writing on caps that went unpunished.

stories.headline: Hungary's Pronatalist Experiment Shows Limits as Fertility Rate Falls Back to Near-2010 Levels
stories.summary:
An in-depth examination of Hungary's sweeping pronatalist policies under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán finds that after an initial rise, the country's fertility rate has fallen to 1.31 in 2025 — barely above the 1.25 recorded when the program launched in 2010, and well below the 2.1 replacement level. The policies, which included interest-free loans, mortgage subsidies, tax breaks, and car grants for married heterosexual couples who pledged to have children, were once hailed by conservative commentators internationally as a model for reversing demographic decline.

Orbán's government rolled out the program after his 2010 re-election, framing it explicitly as an alternative to immigration-based population policy. Fertility did climb to 1.59 by 2020, prompting praise from U.S. and European conservatives. But the rate has since fallen sharply, raising questions about whether financial incentives can produce lasting behavioral change or merely shift the timing of births that would have occurred anyway.

The human cost is visible in cases such as Barbara and Levi Elek of Debrecen, a couple who took a 10-million-forint loan under the program with a promise to have two children. After three rounds of IVF, they face the possibility of repaying the loan with penalty interest if they cannot document a pregnancy by November. Orbán was voted out of office in April 2026; the long-term fate of the subsidy programs under Hungary's new government remains unclear. The findings carry broad relevance as governments across Europe, East Asia, and North America confront declining birth rates.

stories.headline: Update: B-52 Bomber Crashes at Edwards Air Force Base Shortly After Takeoff
stories.summary:
A U.S. Air Force B-52 Stratofortress strategic bomber crashed shortly after takeoff at Edwards Air Force Base in California's Mojave Desert on Monday morning at approximately 11:20 a.m. local time. Emergency crews responded to the scene, which aerial footage showed as a large swath of charred desert with virtually nothing remaining of the aircraft and black smoke rising from the area.

The Air Force and Pentagon confirmed the crash but did not immediately provide information on crew status or casualties. Edwards Air Force Base, located north of Los Angeles, is one of the Air Force's primary flight test centers. The B-52 Stratofortress is a long-range, nuclear-capable strategic bomber produced by Boeing that has been a cornerstone of U.S. airpower for decades.

The cause of the crash was not immediately known. Investigations are ongoing. The B-52 fleet, while aging, has undergone modernization programs and remains central to U.S. strategic deterrence and conventional strike missions globally.

stories.headline: Alaska Election Official Disqualifies Same-Name Challenger to Sen. Dan Sullivan from Primary Ballot
stories.summary:
Alaska's Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher ruled Monday that a man named Dan J. Sullivan is ineligible to appear on the state's August Republican primary ballot as a challenger to incumbent U.S. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. The official concluded that the filing "was not filed in order to declare an actual good-faith candidacy" and represented "a determined effort and a deliberate attempt" to confuse voters.

Republicans had accused Democrats of engineering the same-name candidacy to sow confusion among Republican primary voters in one of the cycle's most competitive Senate races. The disqualified candidate, a retired teacher, has 30 days to appeal the ruling. Ballots are scheduled to be printed on June 28 ahead of the August 18 primary.

The Alaska Senate race is considered among the most watched contests of the 2026 midterm cycle. Democrats denied orchestrating the effort. The ruling removes a potential spoiler from the ballot but the incident has already drawn national attention to ballot integrity questions ahead of the midterms.

stories.headline: South African Jazz Legend Abdullah Ibrahim Dies at 91
stories.summary:
Abdullah Ibrahim, one of the most celebrated figures in South African jazz, died peacefully in Germany on Monday surrounded by family after a short illness, his family announced. He was 91. Born Adolph Johannes Brand in Cape Town in 1934, Ibrahim had a career spanning eight decades and became internationally renowned for blending South African vocal and harmonic traditions with jazz improvisation.

Ibrahim's 1974 composition "Mannenberg" became deeply associated with the anti-apartheid struggle, and his music was considered an act of cultural resistance during the era of legalized racial segregation. He converted to Islam in the late 1960s and changed his name accordingly. American jazz legend Duke Ellington helped bring him to international audiences after hearing him perform in Europe.

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa paid tribute, saying Ibrahim's "creations honoured the South Africa that shaped his political commitment and musical brilliance." His final public performance came at the Cape Town International Jazz Festival less than three months ago. He is survived by his partner, Dr. Marina Umari.

stories.headline: Update: DOJ Opens Investigation into California Governor Gavin Newsom
stories.summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom announced Monday that the U.S. Department of Justice has opened an investigation into him and his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom. Newsom said in a video statement that federal agents had knocked on the doors of family friends and former employees in recent days, demanding records and making use of grand jury processes. The White House declined to comment on the investigation.

Newsom, who is widely expected to launch a 2028 presidential campaign, alleged the inquiry is politically motivated. 'Today, my wife and I joined Donald Trump's hit list,' he wrote on X, asserting that Trump is targeting him because he is considering a presidential run. Supporters characterized the probe as an abuse of executive power.

Critics of the governor, including Republicans, noted that Newsom has been a prominent Trump adversary and a potential 2028 rival, but argued that federal law enforcement agencies have an obligation to investigate credible allegations regardless of the target's political profile. The episode adds to a broader debate over whether the Trump Justice Department has used its prosecutorial power against political opponents.

The investigation's scope and basis have not been disclosed publicly. The development comes as Newsom's term as governor nears its end and as Democratic primary jockeying for 2028 intensifies.

stories.headline: Doctors Without Borders Staff Sexually Abused at Least 59 Sudanese Refugees in Chad
stories.summary:
Medical charity Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has admitted that its staff members sexually abused at least 59 Sudanese refugees in eastern Chad, with some victims being young girls and exploitation often carried out through offers of food or employment in exchange for sex. The offenses date to 2024, approximately one year into Sudan's ongoing civil war, which has driven more than 11 million people from their homes and left 28 million facing acute hunger.

MSF said it has dismissed 18 staff members found responsible but acknowledged it was unable to identify some additional alleged perpetrators. The organization's own internal report from July found patterns of exploitation that could amount to 'sexual trafficking.' Victims who attempted to report the abuse often received no response, and official complaints procedures were described as largely ineffective, with some victims staying silent out of fear that aid would be withheld in retaliation.

'This misconduct represents a serious breach of MSF's values and responsibilities, and we deeply regret the harm caused,' MSF said in response to an investigation by the Associated Press, which first exposed the misconduct. The case is the latest in a series of sexual exploitation scandals to affect international humanitarian organizations operating in conflict zones.

Sudan's civil war, now in its third year, is widely recognized as the world's worst current humanitarian crisis. Estimates of the death toll range from at least 150,000 to as many as 400,000. Mass sexual violence has been extensively documented as a weapon of war in the conflict, making the exploitation of refugees by aid workers particularly grave.

stories.headline: G7 Leaders Gather in France as Trump's Fresh Tariff Threats Overshadow Iran Relief
stories.summary:
Leaders of the Group of Seven nations began arriving Monday at a French lakeside resort for their annual summit, with cautious relief over the U.S.-Iran preliminary peace agreement tempered by new anxiety over President Donald Trump's latest tariff threats. The gathering comes at a moment of acute geopolitical tension, with the Hormuz reopening and ceasefire framework still fragile and trade relations between the U.S. and its closest allies unsettled.

Trump's tariff posture has become a central irritant heading into the summit, with European and other allied governments uncertain about Washington's intentions on trade even as they coordinate on the Iran file. French President Emmanuel Macron is hosting the summit and had planned a Versailles dinner as a backdrop for high-level diplomacy.

The G7 agenda is expected to cover the Iran deal's implementation, Ukraine aid, and global economic coordination, but Trump's bilateral demands on trade have complicated efforts to present a unified front. Allies have repeatedly pressed Washington for clarity on tariff exemptions that remain unresolved.

The summit represents one of the most consequential G7 gatherings in recent years, coinciding with an active Middle East ceasefire process, an ongoing war in Ukraine, and deep uncertainty about the direction of U.S. economic and foreign policy under the second Trump administration.

stories.headline: Brazil Woman Dies After Rope-Jump Instructors Fail to Attach Safety Cord; Three Arrested
stories.summary:
A 21-year-old Brazilian woman died Saturday after rope-jumping instructors at an abandoned bridge in São Paulo state failed to attach a safety cord before letting her leap from a height of approximately 40 meters (130 feet). Maria Eduarda Rodrigues de Freitas fell and was pronounced dead at the scene by emergency services. Video of the incident went viral over the weekend, showing two men in safety helmets holding her by the arms while a third held her feet, with an onlooker screaming for them to attach her cord as she was released.

Three men were arrested in connection with the incident and are under investigation for homicide with eventual intent — a charge used under Brazilian law when a perpetrator does not intend death but consciously assumes the risk of causing it. Local reports indicate the instructors belonged either to a private company offering rope-jumping activities or to informal practitioner groups.

Rope-jumping differs from bungee jumping in that it uses low-stretch climbing ropes to convert a vertical fall into a pendulum swing, requiring precise attachment of the cord before the jump. The bridge, known locally as the Skeleton Bridge, is federally owned but has been abandoned for years. The city of Limeira announced it would sue the federal government for failing to manage the site, calling the death evidence that continued inaction was "unsustainable and unacceptable."

The incident has drawn widespread attention in Brazil and internationally, raising questions about oversight of extreme sports operations at informal or abandoned venues. Brazil's Secretariat of Federal Assets said it was available to assist investigators.

stories.headline: FIFA Investigates Australian VAR Official Over Hand Gesture During World Cup Match
stories.summary:
FIFA is seeking an explanation from Australian video assistant referee Shaun Evans after he was filmed making an inverted "OK" hand gesture on camera before Germany's 7-1 victory over Curacao on Sunday during the World Cup. The gesture, made with his right hand below waist level, has two sharply different interpretations: it is associated with the "circle game," a longstanding internet prank, but has also been co-opted since 2017 as a symbol of white supremacy in far-right circles and was added to the Anti-Defamation League's list of hate symbols in 2019.

The incident triggered immediate and widespread speculation on social media. Anti-discrimination group Fare, which partners with FIFA and UEFA to combat racism, said its experts determined the gesture "clearly resembles an upside down OK hand symbol used as a 'white power' symbol in global far-right circles" and called on FIFA for clarification. Anti-discrimination organization Kick It Out has also written to FIFA seeking answers.

FIFA has not issued a public statement, but sources told BBC Sport the governing body is actively seeking a response from Evans. Notably, FIFA altered its broadcast protocol for subsequent matches: the VAR hub was shown with officials already facing their monitors rather than posing for camera, though their names continued to appear on screen.

Evans, 38, has been on FIFA's referee list since 2017 and is an experienced VAR official. The outcome of FIFA's inquiry — including whether the gesture was intentional, a prank, or innocuous — is expected to be a significant test of how the governing body handles discrimination allegations during the high-profile tournament.

stories.headline: Starbucks Korea to Close All Stores Early Next Week After 'Tank Day' Massacre Controversy
stories.summary:
Starbucks Korea announced Monday that it will close all of its outlets across the country for three hours starting at 3:00 p.m. local time next Wednesday, requiring staff to attend a mandatory historical awareness training session. The closure follows public outrage over a promotional campaign that inadvertently coincided with the anniversary of the 1980 Gwangju Uprising, in which South Korean military forces killed at least 165 civilians — a foundational moment in the country's democracy movement.

The company's "Tank Day" reusable cup promotion, which touted the product's "spacious volume," launched on the anniversary of the massacre. Public anger was swift and severe: South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung denounced the campaign as "inhumane and disgraceful," widespread boycotts were called, the chain reported a significant drop in sales, and Shinsegae Group — which operates Starbucks Korea under a licensing agreement — fired the country's chief executive. The company also acknowledged that an AI tool used to generate marketing slogans contributed to a secondary controversy over promotional language that echoed a notorious 1987 police statement connected to a student activist's death in custody.

All employees will on Monday watch videos covering historical awareness and social sensitivity, with senior leadership including Shinsegae Chairman Chung Yong-jin also scheduled to take the training. It will be the first nationwide early closure of Starbucks Korea since the chain opened in the country in 1999.

The episode highlights growing scrutiny of AI-assisted marketing tools and their potential for culturally insensitive outputs, as well as the acute sensitivity around South Korea's authoritarian past, which remains deeply contested political and social terrain. The Gwangju Uprising is widely regarded as a turning point that ultimately led to the fall of military rule by 1988.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. and Iran Reach Interim Peace Deal; Strait of Hormuz to Reopen, Nuclear Issues Deferred
stories.summary:
The United States and Iran have agreed to an interim peace deal to end 15 weeks of military conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, President Donald Trump and Iranian officials confirmed Sunday. Pakistan, a key mediator, announced that a formal signing ceremony is scheduled for Friday, June 19, in Geneva. The agreement calls for an immediate and permanent halt to military operations 'on all fronts,' including Lebanon, and the lifting of both Iran's closure of the strait and the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The deal leaves the thorniest issues — including verification mechanisms for Iran's nuclear program — to a 60-day follow-on negotiation period. Vice President JD Vance acknowledged on CNBC that 'a lot' of details remain unresolved, while Sen. Lindsey Graham said he is 'concerned' the two sides hold 'different' interpretations of what was agreed. Sen. James Lankford argued the deal should be ratified by Congress for a more lasting effect. Trump told Axios he was 'pissed off' at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for striking Beirut during final negotiations, saying the attack nearly derailed the deal.

Crude oil prices fell more than 4 percent to their lowest levels in over three months following the announcement, reflecting market expectations of eased energy supply. Analysts cautioned that gasoline prices, which had soared to their highest levels since 2022, may remain elevated for months even after the strait fully reopens. European leaders said they stand ready to deploy military assets to help implement the agreement once it is signed.

Key uncertainties remain. Israel has not committed to halting its Lebanon offensive, and Netanyahu has given no indication he will comply with the agreement's ceasefire provisions. Iranian state media and U.S. officials have offered conflicting accounts of what exactly was agreed on nuclear guarantees. The signing ceremony is still several days away, and analysts warn the path to Friday is far from assured.

stories.headline: Fox Corp. to Acquire Roku in $22 Billion Deal, Creating Third-Largest U.S. TV Entity
stories.summary:
Fox Corporation announced Monday it will acquire Roku in a $22 billion cash-and-stock transaction, paying $160 per share. The combined company would rank as the third-largest player in U.S. television by share of viewing, according to Fox. The deal merges Fox's live programming portfolio — including Fox News and broadcast rights to NFL, MLB, and FIFA World Cup events — with Roku's streaming platform, which reaches approximately 100 million U.S. households.

The acquisition is the latest in a sweeping wave of media consolidation as legacy television companies compete for audiences migrating to streaming. Fox previously acquired the Tubi streaming platform in 2020. The deal follows the Justice Department's clearance last week of a $110 billion merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery. Upon close, expected in the first half of 2027, Fox shareholders will own roughly 73 percent of the combined entity and Roku shareholders approximately 27 percent.

Industry analysts have raised concerns that accelerating consolidation could reduce competition, suppress wages for media industry workers, and ultimately raise costs for consumers facing fewer platform choices. The transaction will require regulatory review before it can be completed.

stories.headline: Update: Georgia Special Session Opens Wednesday to Fix Looming Election Law Crisis Before July 1 Deadline
stories.summary:
Georgia lawmakers convene in a special legislative session Wednesday to address a self-created election crisis: the state passed a law two years ago barring the use of QR codes for the official ballot count after July 1, 2026, but never put a replacement vote-counting system in place. With the deadline now days away and a special U.S. House election scheduled for July, conflicting guidance from the secretary of state's office and the State Election Board has left county officials uncertain about how to conduct and tally votes.

Governor Brian Kemp convened the session and directed lawmakers to 'address issues created' by the 2024 law. One likely option is extending the deadline to give the legislature more time to develop a compliant replacement system. Failure to act risks widespread confusion and litigation over elections held after July 1, including the special congressional contest.

The QR code system has been politically contentious since its statewide debut in the 2020 primary. Following President Trump's narrow loss to Joe Biden in Georgia that November, Trump allies claimed without evidence that the machines had switched or deleted votes. Election integrity advocates across the political spectrum also criticized the system, arguing voters cannot verify their choices because QR codes are not human-readable. Trump's first executive order on elections targeted such machines, though courts have blocked its enforcement.

stories.headline: Russian Strikes Kill Nine, Set Historic Kyiv Cathedral Ablaze Ahead of G7
stories.summary:
Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukraine killed at least nine people Monday and set fire to the 11th-century Dormition Cathedral in Kyiv, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Four people died in Kyiv as strikes targeted residential buildings and left more than 140,000 residents without electricity, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Five rescue workers were killed battling a fire caused by a separate strike on Kharkiv in northeastern Ukraine.

The Dormition Cathedral is part of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra monastic complex. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced Ukraine would pursue remedies through UNESCO and other international mechanisms, calling the attack 'state barbarism.' Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko described the assault as brutal. In a retaliatory action, a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian city of Tula killed three people and wounded three others, including a one-year-old child.

The strikes come as most of Ukraine was placed under air raid warnings and as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday he had spoken with U.S. President Donald Trump about efforts to end the conflict. The timing is significant: G7 leaders are meeting in France this week, with the war in Ukraine on the summit agenda. The attack on a UNESCO-listed site is expected to intensify international pressure on Russia.

stories.headline: China Raids Underground Church, Detains Two Leaders During Sunday Service
stories.summary:
Armed police stormed an Early Rain Covenant church service in Jiangyou, southwestern China on Sunday, detaining at least two leaders and taking more than 30 congregants — including children — for questioning. At least 50 officers participated in the raid, which occurred at approximately 11:00 local time while the congregation was meeting in a hotel ballroom. Church leaders Yan Hong and Wu Wuqing remain in detention; the grounds for their arrest have not been disclosed by Chinese authorities.

Early Rain Covenant, founded in Chengdu in 2008, has long been targeted by Chinese authorities, who tightly regulate religious activity and pressure Christians to worship only in state-sanctioned churches. The church's founding pastor, Wang Yi, was detained in a similar raid in December 2018 and is currently serving a nine-year prison sentence. Most congregants taken for questioning were released by late Sunday evening after authorities reportedly attempted — unsuccessfully — to compel them to sign an undisclosed affidavit.

The raid is the latest in a pattern of increased enforcement against unregistered Protestant congregations in China. Bob Fu of the nonprofit ChinaAid said the action reflects the Chinese Communist Party's continued treatment of peaceful Christian worship as a threat to state control. Chinese authorities had not publicly commented on the raid as of Monday.
